A.explanation: Electric field direction is defined as force on a positive charge, so a negative charge feels force $F = qE$ opposite to the field.

B.explanation: A positive charge in an electric field feels a force in the same direction as the field, not opposite.

C.explanation: Gravitational force on any mass is always in the direction of the gravitational field, so it cannot be opposite.

D.explanation: Gravitational force on any mass is always in the direction of the gravitational field, regardless of electric charge sign.

hints: Notice the force is opposite to the field direction, so ask which field always pulls along its own direction for any mass.
Recall electric field direction is defined as the force direction on a positive charge, so $F = qE$ reverses sign when $q$ is negative.
Check whether a gravitational field can ever push opposite to its direction for a normal mass, and then match the sign of charge needed.
walkthrough: Identify the observation: force vector and field vector are in opposite directions in a uniform field.
Recall gravitational field: field strength $g$ is force per unit mass, and force on mass $m$ is $F = mg$ in the same direction as the field for all positive mass.
Therefore a gravitational field cannot give a force opposite to the field, so the field must be electric.
Recall electric field: field strength $E$ is defined as force per unit positive charge, so $F = qE$.
For positive $q$, $F$ is along $E$; for negative $q$, $F$ is opposite to $E$ because $q$ is negative.
The observed opposite direction therefore requires a negative charge in an electric field. This is option A.
